source_review.notes: Reviewed the primary Aggarwal-Vitter I/O-model paper, Vitter's external-memory text, current PostgreSQL and SQLite page-format documentation, the maintainer RocksDB block-format documentation, Linux open(2) direct-I/O constraints, Gray-Graefe's five-minute-rule paper, and CMU's page-storage notes. All eight final destinations returned HTTP 200. Abstract-model results, documented production formats, and chapter design recommendations remain explicitly separated.

evidence: Checked N as external items, M as resident capacity, B as transfer-block capacity, P as optional parallelism, and page/frame/slot identifiers as separate implementation concepts.
Checked Scan(N), Sort(N), tree fan-out/height, byte-region boundaries, page LSN, pin count, dirty state, and generation notation for consistent scope.
Checked ceilings, logarithm base/regime qualifications, encoded-byte units, reserved tails, alignment, and metadata overhead are stated where relevant.
notation_and_syntax.notes: The chapter does not equate an external-memory block with a hardware sector, OS virtual-memory page, filesystem block, or storage-engine page.

evidence: Recomputed the 256-byte model: 32-byte header + four 4-byte slots + 178 payload bytes leaves 30 bytes.
Recomputed deletion and compaction: retiring the 60-byte B record raises contiguous free space from 30 to 90 bytes; inserting E:70 in reused slot 1 leaves 20 bytes.
Recomputed Exercise 2: 4096-128=3968 usable end, 64+4*8=96 metadata, 2400 payload, 1472 contiguous free, and a 1438-byte record-plus-slot leaves 34 bytes.
numerical_recomputation.notes: All byte calculations use the explicitly stated simplified sizes; real alignment, record headers, checksums, and encoding overhead must be included by an implementation.

evidence: Re-derived scan as one transfer per external block, giving Theta(ceil(N/B)).
Re-derived the standard comparison external-sort shape from runs of about M items and merge fan-in about M/B, giving Theta((N/B) log base M/B of N/B) in the nontrivial regime.
Verified slotted-page stable identity follows from preserving page/slot IDs while changing only payload offsets; slot reuse requires a generation or higher-level key validation.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The asymptotic derivations count modeled transfers only and make no latency, CPU, cache, durability, or device-throughput prediction.

evidence: Reviewed empty, exact-fit, full, fragmented, compacted, deleted, reused, growing, shrinking, oversize, overflow-chain, alignment, and maximum-count page states.
Reviewed corrupt magic/type/version/count/offset/length/checksum, arithmetic wrap, overlapping ranges, cycles, duplicate ownership, decompression bombs, hostile bytes, and stale logical identifiers.
Reviewed pin/evict, dirty/WAL, late I/O completion, short/error/torn writes, ENOSPC, allocation/free-list crash points, checkpoint/recovery, migration, and mixed-version boundaries.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: The executable model covers only a finite exclusive-access in-memory subset; the chapter assigns the remaining boundaries to parsers, recovery tests, concurrency models, fuzzing, and fault injection.

evidence: The model checks directory end <= payload start <= page size, live slot bounds, unique nonoverlapping payload offsets, exact payload accounting, and stable four-slot identity.
Delete preserves the slot as a tombstone; compact repacks only live payloads; insert reuses the first tombstone and checks record-plus-slot capacity before mutation.
The chapter separately states page-format, buffer-frame, WAL/durability, allocation, overflow, versioning, and parser-validation invariants.
invariant_checking.notes: The dictionary model is not a byte codec and assumes an exclusive page latch and indivisible operations.

evidence: Reviewed the I/O-model derivation, including the cost unit, scan bound, merge-sort pass structure, regime qualifications, and transfer-to-machine validation boundary.
Reviewed the page-representation argument from encoded regions through checked parsing, mutation, compaction, stable identity, overflow ownership, and version migration.
Reviewed the buffer/durability argument from page/frame identity through pin/latch/dirty state, WAL ordering, write completion, torn-page detection, allocation recovery, and independent inspection.
proof_review.notes: These are scoped design and invariant arguments, not a mechanized proof of a concrete storage engine or filesystem/device durability stack.

evidence: The chapter labels three proof structures and states their assumptions and omitted implementation obligations.
Asymptotic I/O claims are explicitly restricted to the external-memory model; page correctness and durability require additional implementation evidence.
Worked calculations, bounded executable output, cited production formats, testing prescriptions, and deployment recommendations are not presented as interchangeable proof.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No source reachability, checksum, successful model run, or benchmark prescription is generalized into universal correctness or durability.

evidence: The standard-library Python model passed exact twelve-line stdout, empty stderr, and zero exit status under the repository snippet verifier.
It reproduces the 30-to-90-byte compaction change, slot-1 reuse, 20-byte final free region, stable IDs 0..3, active records A/E/C/D, and layout_valid=True.
All eight cited destinations returned HTTP 200 and repository-local structure/link checks passed.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No encoded page, real file I/O, O_DIRECT path, filesystem, device, buffer pool, concurrent mutation, WAL, crash recovery, fuzz campaign, throughput, latency, endurance, or cloud-cost experiment was run.

conceptual_review.notes: The chapter connects external-memory bounds to page layout without conflating abstraction layers, then derives stable slotted-page identity, hostile-input validation, buffering, durability, recovery, migration, and measurement responsibilities.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed format versioning, endian/width rules, checksums, reserved bytes, overflow ownership, buffer state transitions, WAL-before-data, short/torn I/O, allocation recovery, independent tooling, golden fixtures, fuzz/fault tests, benchmarks, observability, rollout, and rollback.

pedagogical_review.notes: The one-page review establishes the model and invariants; the executable page model makes fragmentation and stable slots concrete; ten examples span analytical and operational failures; five exercises provide complete calculations, incident reasoning, format design, and platform-selection answers.

limitations: Internal authoring, primary/maintainer-source, mathematical, bounded executable-model, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical evidence only; no external academic, Aggarwal, Vitter, PostgreSQL, SQLite, RocksDB, Linux, Gray, Graefe, CMU, database, storage-engine, filesystem, kernel, device, reliability, security, performance, or independent practitioner review is claimed. The chapter and model prove neither a concrete byte format, parser, buffer pool, WAL/recovery implementation, allocation map, overflow chain, concurrent execution, crash consistency, corruption tolerance, migration, real I/O complexity, device behavior, performance, cost, certification, nor deployment fitness.
